clinicalPearls: A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is the single most important step; include hobbies, home characteristics, secondhand smoke, and proximity to traffic/industry, plus short- and long-term exposures in the distant past (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Inorganic/organic dust exposure characteristically causes interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity, whereas dusts/chemicals causing occupational asthma or COPD produce airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2234).
A drop in FEV1 measured before vs after a work shift can detect an acute occupational bronchoconstrictive response (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Radiographic pattern hints at etiology: small rounded opacities suggest silicosis or coal worker's pneumoconiosis, while small linear/irregular opacities suggest asbestosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Asbestos exposure causes a spectrum of disease: pleural plaques and benign effusions (marking exposure only), asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), bronchogenic lung cancer, and pleural/peritoneal mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Pleural plaques indicate past asbestos exposure but, by themselves, imply only exposure and not pulmonary impairment (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Smoking and asbestos exposure interact more than additively, producing lung cancer risk greater than the sum of each factor; mesothelioma risk is NOT associated with smoking (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Silicosis raises the risk of mycobacterial (including M. tuberculosis), atypical mycobacterial, and fungal infection because silica impairs alveolar macrophage function; treatment of latent TB is given for a longer duration in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes (seen in up to ~20% of cases) is a characteristic radiographic clue to silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Acute (accelerated) silicosis from very heavy exposure (e.g., sandblasting in confined spaces, denim sandblasting, artificial-stone countertop fabrication) can resemble pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with a 'crazy paving' HRCT pattern and may progress despite stopping exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Chronic beryllium disease mimics sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the distinguishing feature is a beryllium-specific cell-mediated (delayed hypersensitivity) immune response demonstrated by the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Caplan syndrome is the combination of pneumoconiotic nodules and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, first described in coal miners and later in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Documented mesothelioma in a patient with occupational/environmental asbestos exposure may be compensable, as >80% of mesotheliomas are associated with asbestos exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234).
harrison.pathophysiology: Disease depends on the chemical/physical properties of the inhaled agent, which determine dose and site of deposition: water-soluble gases (ammonia, SO2) are absorbed in proximal airways causing irritation/bronchoconstriction, while less-soluble gases (NO2, phosgene) reach bronchioles/alveoli causing chemical pneumonitis. Particles >10-15 micrometres deposit in the nose/throat; particles <10 micrometres reach below the larynx, with coarse-mode (~2.5-10 micrometres, crustal elements like silica) depositing high in the tracheobronchial tree, fine-mode (<2.5 micrometres, from combustion/high-temperature processes) dominating surface area for toxin delivery to lower airways, and ultrafine (<0.1 micrometres, nanoparticles) potentially entering the circulation. Asbestos fibers induce fibrosis through oxidative injury from reactive oxygen species generated by surface transition metals and by phagocytosing cells. Silica causes alveolar macrophage dysfunction (predisposing to infection) and has immunoadjuvant properties (predisposing to autoimmune connective tissue disease). Beryllium drives a CD4+ T-cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation, with susceptibility strongly linked to HLA-DP alleles bearing glutamic acid at position 69 of the beta chain. (Harrison 22e p.2234)
additionalDifferentials: Asbestosis vs other causes of diffuse interstitial fibrosis (IPF/UIP) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Chronic beryllium disease vs sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Silicosis (complicated/PMF) vs coal worker's pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis vs pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) vs influenza or community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Occupational asthma / RADS vs nonoccupational asthma and COPD (Harrison 22e p.2234)
infectionMimics: Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis from thermophilic actinomycete spores) presenting 4-8 h after exposure with fever, chills, malaise, cough, and dyspnea can mimic influenza or pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis with profuse miliary infiltration may radiographically resemble miliary infectious processes (Harrison 22e p.2234)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic beryllium disease closely mimics sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Aluminum and titanium dioxide exposure can produce a sarcoid-like reaction in lung tissue (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Asbestosis mimics idiopathic and other diffuse interstitial fibroses (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Hard-metal (tungsten carbide/cobalt) exposure can cause giant cell interstitial pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
additionalInvestigations: Pre- and post-shift spirometry (change in FEV1) to detect acute bronchoconstriction (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Chest radiograph graded by the ILO International Classification of Radiographs of Pneumoconioses (Harrison 22e p.2234)
CT and high-resolution CT (HRCT) - more sensitive than radiograph for lung opacities, pleural thickening, and interstitial change (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Pulmonary function testing (restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and diffusing capacity in fibrosing disease) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Skin prick testing or specific IgE for immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., flour antigens in bakers) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Specific IgG precipitating antibody titers for hypersensitivity pneumonitis agents (e.g., pigeon antigen in bird handlers) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) for beryllium sensitization (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy (e.g., to diagnose chronic beryllium disease); occasionally video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
redFlags: Mesothelioma may follow relatively short asbestos exposures (<=1-2 years) with latency up to ~40 years - a thorough exposure history is essential (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Lung cancer after asbestos exposure has a minimum latency of ~15-19 years from first exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), occurring in complicated silicosis and CWP, causes severe lung function deficits and is associated with premature mortality; PMF is rising at an alarming rate in the Appalachian coal belt (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Active tuberculosis risk is increased in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis can be severe and progressive even after exposure ceases (Harrison 22e p.2234)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome varies by exposure and disease. Pleural plaques alone do not imply impairment. Simple silicosis and simple CWP are often present without significant functional impairment, but nodular fibrosis can progress even after exposure ceases, coalescing into complicated disease and PMF, which carries severe functional deficits and premature mortality. Acute silicosis may be severe and progressive despite stopping exposure. No specific therapy exists for asbestosis (supportive care as for any diffuse interstitial fibrosis); newly diagnosed cases usually reflect exposures from many years earlier. Asbestos exposure carries excess lung cancer risk (latency ~15-19 years) and mesothelioma risk (latency up to ~40 years). (Harrison 22e p.2234)
pitfalls: Failing to take an occupational/environmental exposure history is the cardinal pitfall - the etiologic link to occupation is missed unless specifically sought, e.g., asking about beryllium exposure in a patient labeled as having sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)

The ILO radiographic classification, though useful for screening populations, is problematic for the individual worker: rounded-opacity disease may look extensive on film with minimal functional impairment, whereas linear/irregular opacities (asbestosis) may lead to underestimation of impairment until late (Harrison 22e p.2234)
In early chronic beryllium disease both chest imaging and pulmonary function tests may be normal (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Attributing dust-related chronic bronchitis/COPD solely to occupation without accounting for cigarette smoking, whose effect is generally additive (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Overlooking that talc and vermiculite may be contaminated with asbestos, conferring fibrosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma risk (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Combat-related embedded metal fragments (shrapnel) in veterans may contain beryllium and serve as an unrecognized exposure source (Harrison 22e p.2234)
harrison.severityClassification: Silicosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis are categorized as simple (small rounded opacities, usually without functional impairment) versus complicated (nodules >=1 cm) which can progress to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF, conglomerate masses >1 cm with restrictive and obstructive impairment). Acute (accelerated) silicosis is distinguished from chronic silicosis by very heavy short-duration exposure and an alveolar-proteinosis-like presentation. Occupational asthma is divided into immunologic (high- vs low-molecular-weight stimuli, with a latency period) and irritative (reactive airway dysfunction syndrome, RADS) forms. (Harrison 22e p.2234)
management: Cessation of and removal from further exposure to the causative dust, fume or fibre, since fibrosing pneumoconioses can progress after exposure ends
Smoking cessation, given the multiplicative lung-cancer risk with asbestos, together with influenza and pneumococcal vaccination

Disease-directed measures where applicable, including inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators for occupational asthma and COPD, and antigen avoidance with corticosteroids for hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Supportive care with pulmonary rehabilitation and long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia
Surveillance for complications, including tuberculosis screening in silicosis and monitoring for lung cancer and mesothelioma after asbestos exposure, with serial spirometry and imaging
Reporting as a notifiable occupational disease with advice on compensation
Referral to respiratory and occupational medicine, with multidisciplinary oncology and palliative care input for malignancy or mesothelioma
